name: Thule Inuit expansion across the Arctic
agents: Thule Inuit (ancestral Inuit), from northern Alaska and the Bering Strait
victims: Late Dorset people (Tuniit)
summary: An expansion case, not a claim that Inuit are foreign colonizers in any modern legal sense. Thule people are the direct ancestors of today's Inuit.
legacy_story: Around 1200 CE, Thule whalers pushed east from Alaska across the Canadian Arctic to Greenland, reaching Ellesmere by mid-century. As they arrived, the Late Dorset, the Tuniit of Inuit oral memory, vanished. Archaeologists still debate how much the two peoples actually met. Thule seem to have salvaged Dorset tools more than lived beside their makers, and ancient DNA finds no Dorset ancestry in the Inuit. Demographic succession is certain. The mechanism is not.

name: Southern Athabaskan (Apachean) migration
agents: Navajo (Diné)
Apache peoples (Western, Chiricahua, Mescalero, Jicarilla, Lipan, Plains Apache)
victims: The Apacheans entered an inhabited Southwest through mixed relations, and the great Puebloan dislocations of the era were caused by Spanish colonization.
summary: An expansion case in the same class as the Thule and Bantu spreads. If anything, the Navajo and Apache became targets of Spanish, Mexican and U.S. settler colonialism, not agents of it.
omission_or_category_error: Migration is well supported, but the present entry itself concedes that Spanish colonization drove the major Puebloan dislocations; it should not imply demonstrated Apachean replacement.
legacy_story: Speakers of Dene languages moved from the western Subarctic of Alaska and northwestern Canada into the American Southwest. Great Basin archaeology, including Dene-style moccasins in Utah's Promontory Caves, places their ancestors on a southern path by the 1200s, and they reached the Colorado Plateau and Rio Grande between roughly 1400 and 1525, shortly before Spanish contact. There they became the Navajo and the Apache, forming new identities through trade, raiding, intermarriage, and the incorporation of Puebloan refugees after the 1680 Pueblo Revolt.

sources.title: Seymour 2012, From the Land of Ever Winter

v4_retirement_reason: The four-century migration umbrella does not define one bounded resident-land displacement outcome; preserve as inactive research context.

name: Teutonic conquest & colonization of Prussia
agents: German-speaking colonists of the Holy Roman Empire
the Teutonic Order
victims: Old Prussians, the Prūsai (Pomesanians, Sambians, Nadruvians and others)
summary: Teutonic conquest & colonization of Prussia, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: In 1226 the Golden Bull of Rimini, an imperial charter from Frederick II, handed the Teutonic Order a crusade against the pagan Old Prussians. Fifty years of war broke them, and the Great Prussian Uprising of 1260–74 was the last serious resistance. Behind the knights came castles, chartered towns under Kulm law, and German-speaking farmers, and the Baltic-speaking Prūsai were killed, subjected, Christianized and slowly absorbed until their language died out entirely by the eighteenth century.

name: Christian colonization of Valencia
agents: Christian settlers from Catalonia and Aragon
victims: Muslim Valencians (Mudéjars)
later Moriscos
summary: A localized medieval case. The later forced conversions and the 1609 expulsion of the Moriscos belong to a longer history not shown here as one continuous phase.
legacy_story: When James I of Aragon took Valencia in 1238, scribes wrote the colonization down in the Llibre del Repartiment, house by house and field by field, the property of a Muslim kingdom handed to Christian settlers from Catalonia and Aragon. The newcomers ruled as a minority over a Mudéjar majority for generations, colonial settlement without immediate demographic replacement. Robert Burns called it exactly that, medieval colonialism, the exploitation of a subject population through tax and lordship.

sources.title: Bulletin critique des Annales islamologiques, review of El naixement d'una colònia: domination and resistance in Valencia, 1238–1276

name: Norse settlement of Greenland
agents: Norse Greenlanders (Grœnlendingar), from Iceland and western Norway
victims: None. Southern Greenland held no one when the Norse arrived, the earlier Saqqaq and Dorset having left centuries before
Thule Inuit, spreading south into the same Arctic hunting grounds from about 1200, met and contested by the Norse but never displaced by them
summary: Norse settlement of Greenland, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: The Norse settled areas apparently unoccupied at arrival and later overlapped with Thule Inuit; this is settlement history, not demonstrated displacement by the Norse.
legacy_story: A settler colony that failed and left no one to mourn it. Around 985 Erik the Red, exiled from Iceland, led farmers into a southwest Greenland empty of people. At its height the colony held two to three thousand settlers, a bishop at Garðar, and an export trade in walrus ivory that sent hunters far up the coast. There they met the Thule Inuit, who were spreading south across the Arctic from about 1200, and the sagas record both trade and killing with the people they called skrælingar. Then the Little Ice Age bit, the ivory market collapsed, and the coastal fields failed. The last record is a wedding at Hvalsey in 1408, and it was the Thule, better suited to the cooling Arctic, who remained.

sources.title: Star et al. 2018 (Proc. R. Soc. B)

v4_retirement_reason: Initial Norse settlement occurred on land not shown to have a resident population displaced in or around 985; preserve as an inactive boundary example.

name: Vietnamese southward expansion (Nam tiến)
agents: Kinh (Việt) settlers under Đại Việt and the Nguyễn
victims: Cham (Chăm)
Khmer / Khmer Krom
summary: The familiar image of one smooth “southward march” hides long pauses and sharp regional differences.
omission_or_category_error: A 763-year umbrella conflates conquest of Cham polities, Vietnamese settler movement, incorporation of the Mekong delta, and later Nguyễn state colonization; each phase affected different peoples and places.
legacy_story: Over seven centuries the Vietnamese state moved south, absorbing the Cham and Khmer lands along the coast. The hinge was 1471, when Lê Thánh Tông stormed the Cham capital Vijaya. Vietnamese annals claim 60,000 killed and 30,000 taken, an event George Dutton frames as the genocide of Champa. Nguyễn lords then colonized the Khmer Mekong delta, including Prey Nokor, the future Saigon, before Minh Mạng annexed the last Cham principality in 1832.

name: Inca resettlement system (mitma)
agents: Mitmaqkuna (Inca state colonists)
victims: Quechua (Runa)
Aymara
Cañari
Chachapoya
Colla & Lupaca
summary: Inca resettlement system (mitma), as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: The Inca colonized from within. From Pachacuti's reign the state uprooted whole communities, the mitmaqkuna, and transplanted them across Tawantinsuyu. Loyal colonists were planted among the newly conquered, rebels scattered far from home, farmers moved to open the maize estates of the Cochabamba valley. Cañari and Chachapoya potters carried Cusco techniques a thousand kilometres north, a physical trace of forced migration. The Spanish conquest shattered the system, and the displaced tried to walk home.

name: Canary Islands
agents: Castilians and Andalusians
Norman adventurers under Castile
Portuguese and Genoese planters
victims: Guanches (Tenerife), Canarios (Gran Canaria) and other Indigenous Canary Islanders
summary: The marker locates the archipelago. Conquest ran island by island across most of a century.
legacy_story: Europe's first overseas settler genocide, in Mohamed Adhikari's phrase. Conquest opened in 1402 when Norman lords in Castilian service seized Lanzarote, and crown armies finished Gran Canaria, La Palma and finally Tenerife, where the last Guanche kings surrendered in 1496. The Indigenous islanders, Berber-descended peoples across the archipelago, were killed, enslaved, deported and absorbed until they no longer existed as distinct nations. Settlers from Castile, Portugal and Genoa took the ground.

name: Plantations of Ireland
agents: English and Welsh planters (New English)
Lowland Scots (Ulster Scots)
London livery companies
victims: Gaelic Irish (Gaeil)
Old English Catholic landholders
summary: Plantations of Ireland, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: Laois–Offaly, Munster, Ulster, and Cromwellian confiscation were separate projects with different dates, sponsors, settler streams, and removals.
legacy_story: England colonized Ireland by planting it. The policy opened under Mary I with Laois–Offaly in 1556, ran through Munster after the Desmond wars, and reached its scale in Ulster from 1609, where six escheated counties were parcelled to English and Scottish settlers. By 1641 perhaps 100,000 British migrants had arrived, tens of thousands of them Lowland Scots. Catholic-held land fell from around three-fifths of the island to a seventh by 1703 as war and confiscation did their work.

name: Spanish settlement in the northern borderlands
agents: Spanish and mixed-descent pobladores from New Spain
Franciscan missionaries and presidio soldiers
victims: Pueblo nations (Tewa, Tiwa, Keres, Zuni, Hopi)
Ohlone
Chumash
Kumeyaay
Comanche & Apache
summary: A qualified regional case. The 1848 endpoint marks U.S. acquisition, not the end of colonial effects.
omission_or_category_error: The northern borderlands entry does not cover the much larger Spanish conquest, Indigenous demographic collapse, congregation, labor coercion, and settler land transfer in Mesoamerica and the Andes.
legacy_story: New Spain reached north through missions, presidios and ranches into Pueblo, Ohlone, Chumash and Kumeyaay homelands. Oñate's 1598 entry into New Mexico and the 1599 Acoma massacre set the tone, and the 1680 Pueblo Revolt under Po'pay expelled the colonists for twelve years before the reconquest. Franciscans built the twenty-one Alta California missions from 1769. But Comanche and Apache power kept the borderlands thin, and settlement stayed sparse outside a few corridors until the United States took the region in 1848.

sources.title: Akins & Bauer 2021, We Are the Land

v4_retirement_reason: The 1598–1848 regional wrapper spans multiple territories, peoples, and mechanisms; its ordinal scores cannot be source-traced or arithmetically stripped of the bounded Southwest successors. Preserve it as an inactive umbrella and replace it only with source-bounded events.

name: Volga–Ural & Bashkir lands
agents: Russian peasant colonists
nobles buying alienated land
Orenburg Cossacks
victims: Bashkirs (Basqorttar)
summary: Volga–Ural & Bashkir lands, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: The case compresses imperial annexation, repeated Bashkir uprisings, land-survey expropriation, factory and peasant settlement, and nineteenth-century agrarian colonization into one undifferentiated arc.
legacy_story: After Kazan fell in 1552 the Bashkirs kept their patrimonial land rights on paper, and lost them in practice. Forts at Ufa and Orenburg anchored colonization, and revolt after revolt was crushed, in 1662, 1704, 1735–40, and again under Salawat Yulayev in the Pugachev rising. Between 1869 and 1878 alone the state alienated nearly a million desiatinas of Bashkir land through forced sales. Edyta Bojanowska's study shows even Tolstoy buying Bashkir steppe cheap while its nomads were pushed off.

name: Circassia
agents: Kuban & Black Sea Cossacks
Russian and Ukrainian peasant colonists
victims: Circassians / Adyghe
Ubykh
Abazins
Abkhaz
summary: Circassia, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: The end of the Russo-Circassian war in 1864 was also the emptying of a homeland. When the last resistance broke at Qbaada above Sochi, Russia expelled the Adyghe wholesale to the Ottoman Empire. Walter Richmond estimates at least 600,000 dead of massacre, starvation and exposure, roughly three-quarters of the Circassian people. The survivors scattered to Turkey, Jordan and Syria, and Cossack colonists settled the cleared coast.

name: Kazakh Steppe
agents: Russian and Ukrainian peasant settlers
Cossack hosts
victims: Kazakhs (Qazaqtar)
summary: Kazakh Steppe, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: Imperial conquest, Cossack lines, late-imperial peasant colonization, Soviet collectivization and famine, and later demographic engineering are distinct processes; the existing case hides the breaks.
legacy_story: Russian protection over the Kazakh khans, sworn in 1731, hardened into land seizure. Roughly 1.5 million settlers from European Russia and Ukraine took the pasture in the late-tsarist colonization surge, and the khanates were abolished outright. Then Soviet collectivization brought famine: Sarah Cameron finds about 1.5 million dead in 1930–33, some 1.3 million of them Kazakhs, proportionally the worst toll of any Soviet nationality. It left Kazakhs a minority in their own republic for decades.

name: Russian Far East
agents: Amur & Ussuri Cossacks
Russian and Ukrainian peasant settlers
victims: Nanai (Nani)
Udege
Ulch
Nivkh
Orochi
Negidal
Evenki
summary: Russian Far East, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: Annexation from Qing China, Cossack and peasant settlement, Indigenous dispossession, anti-Chinese violence, Korean removal, and Soviet security deportations cannot be treated as one event.
legacy_story: The treaties of Aigun and Peking, 1858–60, handed Russia the Amur and Ussuri from a weakened Qing, and the Cossack hosts moved onto the river line. Subsidized steamship passage from Odesa filled it fast. By 1913 about 250,000 peasants had arrived, three-quarters of them Ukrainian, which gave the settlement belt its name, Zelenyi Klyn, the Green Wedge. The Nanai, Udege, Nivkh and Orochi became small minorities, and in 1937 the Soviet state deported 172,000 Koreans to Central Asia to finish reordering the coast.

name: Sápmi
agents: Swedish and Finnish agrarian settlers
Norwegian farmers and fishers
Russian/Soviet industrial settlers on Kola
victims: Sámi (Sámit / Sápmelaccaš)
summary: Sápmi, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: Four states used different settlement, taxation, schooling, mining, border-closure, and land policies over several centuries; a single cross-border case erases those differences.
legacy_story: Four states enclosed the Sámi north. Swedish colonization pushed in from the 1630s with silver mining at Nasafjäll, which conscripted Sámi to haul ore by reindeer, and a 1673 proclamation then invited farmers onto Sámi taxed lands. Norway's Norwegianization ran from 1851 to the 1980s, banning the language in schools, while Sweden's nomad-school policy kept reindeer-herding Sámi in separate, inferior classrooms. Åsa Össbo reads the mining, the hydropower dams and today's wind farms as one long industrial colonialism.

sources.title: Settler Colonial Studies, From Indigenous private property to full dispossession: the case of Sápmi

name: Han settlement of Taiwan
agents: Hoklo (southern Fujianese) migrants
Hakka from Guangdong
victims: Plains (Pingpu) peoples such as Siraya and Babuza
mountain nations such as Atayal, Paiwan and Bunun
summary: Han settlement of Taiwan, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: Dutch recruitment, Zheng military settlement, Qing frontier expansion, and Japanese colonial land policy are not one continuous Han settlement event; Indigenous land loss must be periodized.
legacy_story: Han Taiwan grew from a few thousand to a few million in two centuries. Hoklo migrants from Fujian and Hakka from Guangdong crossed the strait under the Dutch, the Zheng regime and then the Qing, and a Qing count in 1811 recorded 1.9 million people, overwhelmingly Han. The plains Austronesian peoples, the Siraya, Babuza and others, lost their land through Qing leasing and mortgage law and were absorbed, while the mountain nations held out until Japanese campaigns after 1895.

name: Dzungaria
agents: Han & Hui farmers from Gansu-Shaanxi
Manchu, Sibe & Chahar bannermen
Taranchi Uyghurs
victims: Zünghars (Oirat / western Mongols)
summary: The incoming population was deliberately mixed, not a Han-only movement.
omission_or_category_error: The destruction of the Dzungar polity and population, postwar repopulation by multiple groups, and later military-agricultural colonization are causally linked but distinct events.
legacy_story: The Qing did not just conquer the Zünghars. They erased them. In 1755–58 the Qianlong emperor's armies, aided by smallpox, destroyed the Oirat Mongol state of Dzungaria, and Peter Perdue and others estimate that 70–80% of the population died or fled, on the order of half a million people. Then the Qing repopulated the emptied land from 1759 with Han and Hui farmers, Manchu and Sibe bannermen, and Taranchi Uyghur cultivators. It was a deliberate colonization of a cleared frontier.

name: Han settlement of Inner Mongolia
agents: Han Chinese farmers and, later, state-organized migrants
victims: Mongols (Öbür Mongghol, incl. Chahar, Ordos and Bargas)
summary: Han settlement of Inner Mongolia, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: Late-Qing cultivation policy, Republican-era migration, PRC state farms, collectivization, and post-1978 urban expansion have different institutions and local effects.
legacy_story: Inner Mongolia became a Han land through the plow. From about 1902 the late-Qing “New Policies” reversed the old ban and opened Mongol banner pasture to farming, pushing herders toward sedentarization and provoking the duguilang revolts. Warlords and settlers kept coming, and then the PRC drove large-scale in-migration from the 1950s through state farms and industry. Mongols, roughly a fifth of the region in 1949, fell to about 17–18% of some 24 million people, a minority in their own autonomous region.

sources.title: Bulag 2002, The Mongols at China’s Edge

name: Han in-migration in Tibetan areas
agents: Han Chinese migrants (cadres, workers, traders) and state personnel
victims: Tibetans (Böpa)
summary: Han in-migration in Tibetan areas, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: The entry must distinguish voluntary and state-facilitated migration, military-administrative control, pastoralist relocation, boarding schools, and disputed claims of demographic replacement.
legacy_story: The People's Liberation Army entered eastern Tibet in 1950, and the Seventeen Point Agreement formalized Chinese sovereignty in 1951. Emily Yeh's Taming Tibet shows how state development remade Lhasa and drew Han traders and workers into its economy, accelerated by the Qinghai–Tibet railway in 2006. Han remain a minority in the Tibet Autonomous Region proper, and Andrew Fischer reads the 2020 census at about 12%, but they dominate its towns and are far more numerous in the Tibetan areas of Qinghai and Sichuan.

name: Hokkaidō
agents: Wajin (ethnic Japanese) migrants, especially from Tōhoku
farmer-soldier colonists
victims: Ainu
summary: Hokkaidō, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: Meiji settler colonization, land survey and dispossession, assimilation, and twentieth-century development are presented as one open-ended process without separating policy shifts or Ainu regions.
legacy_story: In 1869 the Meiji state annexed Ezo, renamed it Hokkaidō, and set up a Colonization Commission that spent 20 million yen settling the island. From 1874 samurai-farmer militia colonists took Ainu land, and the population passed a million by 1901. The 1899 Former Aborigines Protection Act gave Ainu poorer farmland and forced Japanese schooling, and stood until 1997. Only in 2019 did Japan recognize the Ainu as an Indigenous people, and a survey counts about 13,000, widely thought an undercount.

name: Japanese Korea
agents: Japanese civilian settlers (merchants, officials and farmers)
victims: Koreans (dominated and dispossessed in place)
summary: Japanese Korea, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: Japanese settlers reached Korea from the 1876 treaty ports, three decades before annexation, and some 170,000 were already there in 1910. Jun Uchida calls them the brokers of empire. Their number neared 700,000 by the 1940s, one of the century's largest colonial settler communities, expanding on the back of a 1910–18 cadastral survey and the Oriental Development Company's landholdings. In 1945 nearly all of them were repatriated, reversing the settlement order in a single year.

name: Manchuria / Manchukuo
agents: Japanese agricultural colonists (incl. a youth brigade)
urban civilians of the railway zone
victims: Chinese (Han) & Manchu farmers
Korean tenant cultivators
Mongol pastoralists
summary: The projected scale was never reached. This is an attempted mass colonization more than a completed one.
omission_or_category_error: Japanese railway-zone settlement, the puppet-state colonization program, mass agrarian migration, and wartime forced labor need separate treatment; the 1905 start predates Manchukuo by decades.
legacy_story: Japan planned to plant five million settlers in Manchuria and managed a fraction of it. The 1936 “million households” scheme aimed to make Japanese a tenth of the population, but actual agricultural colonists reached only about 270,000–320,000 by 1945, their land taken from Chinese and Korean farmers at forced prices. When the Soviets invaded in August 1945, roughly a third of the settlers died in the flight and the winter that followed, and thousands of children were left behind in China.

name: Japanese Micronesia
agents: Japanese home-island migrants
Okinawan farm and fishing families
Korean labourers, many of them coerced
victims: CHamoru & Refaluwasch (Northern Marianas)
Palauans
Chuukese, Pohnpeians, Yapese, Kosraeans
Marshallese
summary: Japanese Micronesia, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: Japan seized Germany's Micronesian islands in 1914 and ran them as the Nan'yō. Sugar drew settlers by the tens of thousands, most from Okinawa: by 1937 Japanese outnumbered Islanders across the whole mandate, about 62,000 to 50,000, and Saipan's Garapan was nearly all Japanese. In Palau, incomers were 60% of the population by 1935. Japan's 1945 defeat repatriated almost all of them, and the settler order collapsed as fast as it had risen.

name: Andaman Islands
agents: Convicts and their descendants
Partition-era Bengali refugees
mainland labourers and migrants
victims: Great Andamanese
Onge
Jarawa
Sentinelese
summary: Andaman Islands, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: British penal colonization and post-independence Indian refugee and development settlement were distinct regimes affecting different islands and Indigenous peoples.
legacy_story: Britain founded the Port Blair penal colony in 1858 to hold rebels of 1857, and the settlement it seeded destroyed the islanders. The Great Andamanese collapsed from several thousand at contact to 625 by 1901 and an all-time low of 19 in 1961, wrecked by measles, influenza and syphilis. After 1947 India settled Partition refugees and mainland labourers, and some 400,000 people now vastly outnumber a few hundred Great Andamanese, Onge, Jarawa and Sentinelese, whose forests a trunk road still cuts through.

name: Mindanao
agents: Christian Filipino homesteaders from Luzon and the Visayas
victims: Moro peoples (Maguindanao, Maranao, Tausūg, Iranun)
Lumad peoples (Manobo, T'boli, B'laan, Subanen)
summary: Mindanao, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: US colonial land policy, Commonwealth settlement agencies, postwar migration, logging and plantation concessions, and conflict displacement are distinct processes with different affected Moro and Lumad communities.
legacy_story: State-backed settlement turned a Muslim island into a Christian-majority one. American authorities opened agricultural colonies in Cotabato from 1913. The Commonwealth's National Land Settlement Administration followed in 1939, and Magsaysay's EDCOR resettled ex-rebels and soldiers from Luzon in the 1950s. Around 1.2 million migrants entered in 1948–60 alone. The Moro peoples fell from roughly three-quarters of Mindanao's population at 1900 to about a quarter by 1948, and the Lumad to a small minority, their customary land redefined as public.

name: Vietnam's Central Highlands
agents: Kinh (ethnic Vietnamese) migrants from the Red River Delta and lowlands
victims: Degar / Montagnard peoples such as Ê Đê (Rhade), Jarai, Bahnar, Kơho and Mnông
summary: Vietnam's Central Highlands, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: South Vietnamese resettlement, wartime displacement, post-1975 New Economic Zones, coffee expansion, and state-farm land seizure are not one uninterrupted event.
legacy_story: After the 1954 partition, Diem's government began resettling lowland Kinh, including northern Catholic refugees, in the highlands. By 1975 perhaps a million had moved in, and after reunification New Economic Zone and spontaneous migration brought up to three million more, while the 1990s coffee boom drove smallholders onto Indigenous land. The Degar or Montagnard peoples (Ê Đê, Jarai, Bahnar and others) are now perhaps a third of the region, and their 2001 land protests met a hard crackdown.

name: Chittagong Hill Tracts
agents: Bengali settlers from the plains districts of Bangladesh
victims: Jumma peoples such as Chakma, Marma, Tripura, Mru and Bawm
summary: Chittagong Hill Tracts, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: Bangladesh moved its lowlanders uphill. A covert state program from 1979 to 1984 shifted more than 400,000 Bengali settlers into the Chittagong Hill Tracts with land grants and rations, and the Bengali share of the population jumped from 12% in 1974 to nearly half by 1991. The 1962 Kaptai Dam had already drowned 40% of the best farmland and displaced 100,000 people, mostly Chakma. Counter-insurgency against the Jumma peoples brought massacres through the 1980s and 90s, and the 1997 peace accord's land promises remain largely unmet.

name: Sri Lankan irrigation settlements
agents: Sinhalese peasant colonists from the south and centre, state-sponsored
victims: Sri Lankan Tamils of the northern/eastern dry zone
Muslims of contested eastern districts
summary: Sri Lankan irrigation settlements, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: Gal Oya, Mahaweli, Weli Oya, and other schemes had different dates, sponsors, ethnic politics, and displacement footprints; one national label is not an event-level account.
legacy_story: Sri Lanka colonized its own dry zone. State-aided schemes from the 1935 Land Development Ordinance moved Sinhalese peasants into districts Tamils and Muslims claimed, redrawing the electoral map, and Patrick Peebles reads the whole program as a driver of the ethnic conflict. The sharpest case is Weli Oya, carved out of Tamil-majority Manal Aru in 1984 and militarized. Tamil residents got 48-hour eviction notices, and by 2012 the area's 18 villages were 99.7% Sinhalese. The war it fed brought massacres on both sides.

name: West Papua
agents: Javanese and Madurese transmigrants
Bugis, Makassarese and Butonese migrants
victims: Papuans (Melanesian peoples, incl. the Moi of Sorong)
summary: West Papua, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: Military occupation, formal transmigration, spontaneous migration, resource concessions, urban land seizure, and conflict displacement require separate dates and evidentiary claims.
legacy_story: Indonesia took West Papua's administration in 1963 and ratified it through the 1969 “Act of Free Choice,” a vote of 1,022 hand-picked electors. Non-Papuans were 4% of the population in 1971. By 2010, after decades of transmigration and spontaneous migration from Java and Sulawesi, settlers were a slight majority overall, and Jim Elmslie projected the Indigenous share falling below 30%. New transmigration plans floated in 2024 drew fresh Papuan protest. The highlands remain overwhelmingly Papuan. The coasts and towns do not.

name: Namibia
agents: German settlers and Schutztruppe veterans
Afrikaner and other white South Africans
victims: Herero (Ovaherero)
Nama
Damara
San
summary: Namibia, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: German conquest, the Herero and Nama genocide, settler land allocation, and South African mandate/apartheid rule were distinct regimes; ending only at independence hides the changing machinery.
legacy_story: Germany declared a protectorate in 1884 and built its only true settler colony on the land it seized. When the Herero rose in 1904 and the Nama followed, General von Trotha issued an extermination order. By 1908 roughly 65,000 Herero, four in five, and at least 10,000 Nama were dead by shooting, thirst in the Omaheke, and the camps at Shark Island. South Africa took over in 1915 and extended apartheid until independence in 1990. Germany acknowledged the genocide only in 2021.

name: Southern Rhodesia / Zimbabwe
agents: British settlers
white South Africans
other European migrants
victims: Shona (Zezuru, Karanga, Manyika)
Ndebele
Tonga
summary: Southern Rhodesia / Zimbabwe, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company sent a Pioneer Column into Mashonaland in 1890, and war finished the conquest, the Ndebele kingdom in 1893 and the Shona and Ndebele risings of 1896–97. The 1930 Land Apportionment Act handed roughly half the colony to about 48,000 whites, under 5% of the people. Ian Smith declared independence in 1965 to preserve minority rule, and the settler population peaked near 300,000 before the liberation war ended the settler state at Zimbabwe's independence in 1980.

name: Kenya Highlands
agents: British settler farmers
South African and other European migrants
victims: Kikuyu (Gĩkũyũ)
Maasai
Nandi and other Kalenjin
Kamba
summary: Kenya Highlands, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: Britain reserved Kenya's best land for whites and called it the White Highlands. Crown Lands ordinances from 1902 let settlers take 999-year leases, and the 1939 Highlands Order fenced roughly 7.5 million acres off from Africans, policed by a board that vetted every sale. The Maasai were moved south by “agreement” in 1904 and 1911. Over 200,000 Kikuyu lived as squatter-labourers on settler farms, and their eviction and land hunger fed the Mau Mau uprising and the emergency of 1952–60.

name: Liberia
agents: Free-born and freed African Americans (Americo-Liberians)
recaptured Africans ('Congoes')
victims: Kpelle
Bassa
Grebo
Kru
Vai
Gola and other Indigenous Liberian peoples
summary: Liberia, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: A settler colony of freed slaves. The American Colonization Society planted its first settlers at Cape Mesurado in 1822, and by 1867 had sent more than 13,000 African American emigrants. The colony declared itself a republic in 1847 with a constitution written by and for the settler class. The Americo-Liberians, a few percent of the population, ruled the Indigenous majority through the True Whig Party from 1878 until Samuel Doe's 1980 coup ended their monopoly, a distinctive Black, non-metropolitan case of the same structure.

name: Argentina: Pampas & Patagonia
agents: Argentine criollo settlers and military colonists
Italian, Spanish and other European immigrants
victims: Mapuche
Ranquel (Rankülche)
Tehuelche (Aónikenk)
Günün a küna
summary: Buenos Aires stands for the state and the migration gateway. The Chaco frontier followed a distinct chronology not folded in here.
legacy_story: Argentina cleared its south by campaign. Law 215 of 1867 set the conquest of the Indigenous frontier as state policy, and from 1878 General Roca's Conquest of the Desert drove it home with breech-loading rifles, killing and capturing thousands of Mapuche, Ranquel and Tehuelche and interning prisoners on Martín García island. The last cacique, Sayhueque, surrendered in 1885. The conquered land, some 8.5 million hectares from one campaign's bonds, went to a few hundred owners and to the European immigrants pouring through Buenos Aires.

name: Chile: Araucanía
agents: Chilean settlers from central Chile
German, Swiss, Italian and Boer colonists
victims: Mapuche of Gülumapu (Nagche, Wenteche and Lafkenche)
summary: Chile: Araucanía, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: For two centuries Spain recognized Mapuche autonomy south of the Biobío, and Chile ended it by force. Colonel Saavedra's occupation of Araucanía, planned from 1861, advanced with forts and towns. The last general Mapuche uprising broke in 1881, and the re-founding of Villarrica in 1883 closed the conquest. The state then penned Mapuche communities into some 3,000 reducciones, about 500,000 hectares of their former country, and handed the rest to Chilean and European colonists, Germans and Swiss and Boers among them.

name: Uruguay
agents: Spanish and Italian immigrants
the Uruguayan criollo state
victims: Charrúa
Minuán
Guaraní
summary: A qualified case. The displaced Charrúa were a small, mobile population, and Uruguay's settler majority came mostly from later European immigration rather than from replacing a large Indigenous society.
omission_or_category_error: The Salsipuedes campaign and subsequent removal, captivity, land privatization, and transborder Indigenous survival need their own bounded events; '1831–20th century' is not a usable chronology.
legacy_story: Uruguay built its European self-image on a massacre. On 11 April 1831, President Fructuoso Rivera's forces ambushed the Charrúa at Salsipuedes, killing about 40 and taking 300 prisoner, and four captives were shipped to Paris in 1833 and exhibited. Mass Spanish and Italian immigration then filled the country and let the state call itself a país sin indios, a land without Indians. It was never true, and Charrúa descendants organized from 1989 and now contest the story of their own extinction.

name: Mennonite Chaco, Paraguay
agents: Mennonites from Canada (1927)
Mennonites from the Soviet Union (1930, 1947)
victims: Enlhet Norte & Enxet Sur
Nivaclé
Ayoreo (incl. Totobiegosode)
Guaraní Ñandeva
summary: Mennonite Chaco, Paraguay, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: A settler colony with no metropole behind it. Paraguay's 1921 law promised Mennonites exemption from military service, oaths and state schooling, and in 1927 the first 1,743 pioneers from Canada founded Menno Colony in the Chaco, and refugees from the Soviet Union followed in 1930 and 1947. The colonies occupy Enlhet, Nivaclé and Ayoreo land, and their cooperatives now run the central Chaco's cattle-and-dairy economy while some Ayoreo-Totobiegosode still live in voluntary isolation in the shrinking forest.

name: Bolivian eastern lowlands
agents: Andean Quechua and Aymara colonists
Mennonite and Okinawan colonies
agribusiness migrants
victims: Guaraní
Ayoreo
Chiquitano (Monkoxi)
Guarayo
Yuracaré
Mojeño
summary: Bolivian eastern lowlands, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: Santa Cruz colonization, Mennonite settlement, cattle and soy frontiers, road building, and distinct Indigenous territorial conflicts cannot be represented by one national lowlands case.
legacy_story: Bolivia turned east after its 1952 revolution. The US-backed Plan Bohan had drawn the blueprint, and the 1953 agrarian reform and later governments opened colonization corridors in Santa Cruz and the Chapare, moving Andean Quechua and Aymara settlers, plus state-recruited Mennonite and Okinawan colonies, into the lowlands. Ben Nobbs-Thiessen traces how this remade Santa Cruz into an agro-industrial heartland, and the two colonization zones account for most of Bolivia's deforestation, at the expense of Guaraní, Ayoreo and Chiquitano land.

name: New Caledonia
agents: French convicts and free settlers (Caldoches)
Communard and Algerian deportees who stayed
victims: Kanak (Melanesian clans of Grande Terre and the Loyalty Islands)
summary: New Caledonia, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: France annexed New Caledonia in 1853 and settled it partly with convicts, some 22,000 transported to 1897, including 4,250 Communards. Land ceded to colonists rose from 1,000 hectares in 1860 to 230,000 by 1878, the year Grand Chief Ataï's revolt was crushed at the cost of a thousand Kanak lives. Governor Feillet then cut the Kanak reserves from 320,000 to 120,000 hectares. The Kanak, reduced from perhaps 60,000 to 27,000 by 1900, are now about 40% of the population, and three independence referendums have failed.

sources.title: International Journal of the Commons, Kanak land dispossession and contemporary commons in New Caledonia

name: Hawaiʻi
agents: New England missionary families and descendants
the Euro-American planter and military elite
later U.S. settlers
victims: Kānaka Maoli (Native Hawaiians)
summary: Hawaiʻi, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: Missionary-commercial settlement, the Māhele land regime, overthrow and annexation, plantation labor importation, military land taking, and post-statehood development are distinct processes.
legacy_story: New England missionaries arrived in 1820 and their families became Hawaiʻi's landholding, sugar-growing elite. The 1848 Māhele broke up the traditional land system and let foreigners buy in, and many makaʻāinana ended up with nothing. In 1893 a committee of planters overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani with U.S. Marines behind them. A petition of 21,000 Kānaka Maoli, more than half those counted, defeated the annexation treaty, so Congress annexed the islands by simple resolution in 1898. The Native population had fallen from perhaps 300,000 at contact to about 40,000.

name: Guam / Guåhan
agents: Spanish garrison and missionaries (1668–1898)
U.S. military and federal personnel
post-war civilian migrants
victims: CHamoru people of Guåhan
summary: Guam / Guåhan, as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: Spanish reduccion and depopulation, US naval rule and land acquisition, Japanese wartime occupation, and postwar military expansion are separate displacement regimes.
legacy_story: Guam was colonized twice. Spain's conquest from 1668 imposed the reducción, and war and disease cut the CHamoru to about 3,500 by 1710. The United States took the island in 1898 and layered a second colonization over the first. After retaking Guam in 1944, the U.S. military seized 52,000 acres and at its peak held 63% of Guåhan, condemning most of it in 1948 at pre-war prices. Roughly 28% remains under military control, and the CHamoru are a minority on their own island, in an unincorporated territory whose residents still cannot vote for president.

name: Rapa Nui
agents: European ranchers (Williamson-Balfour Company)
the Chilean state, navy and mainland migrants
victims: Rapanui
summary: The 1862–63 slave raids and first ranching predate the 1888 annexation that opens this record.
legacy_story: Rapa Nui nearly disappeared before Chile ever raised its flag. Peruvian slavers seized over 1,400 people in 1862–63, a third to a half of the island, and the smallpox the few survivors carried home killed roughly a thousand more, dropping the population to about 100. Chile annexed the island in 1888, then leased it to a Scottish-Chilean sheep company that penned the Rapanui behind a wall at Hanga Roa until the 1960s. Only the 1966 Ley Pascua gave them citizenship and the run of their own island.

name: Vanuatu / New Hebrides
agents: French planters and land companies
British and Australian planters
condominium officials
victims: ni-Vanuatu (Indigenous Melanesian peoples)
summary: Vanuatu / New Hebrides, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: The New Hebrides were worked over twice: labour taken out, planters moved in. Between 1863 and 1904, blackbirding carried more than 60,000 South Sea Islanders to Queensland's plantations, many of them ni-Vanuatu. French and British planters then alienated so much land that by the mid-twentieth century over a third of the islands was foreign-owned, though the ni-Vanuatu stayed the majority. At independence in 1980, the new constitution reversed a century of it in one line: all land belongs to the indigenous custom owners.

name: Banaba (Ocean Island)
agents: Imported mine labourers (Chinese and Pacific Islander) under the phosphate regime
victims: Banabans (te aomata ni Banaba), forcibly resettled to Rabi, Fiji in 1945
summary: Banaba (Ocean Island), as represented in the current atlas.
omission_or_category_error: Mining-induced removal of Banabans to Rabi was not a settler colony, but calling it excluded erases a severe, land-destroying displacement; it belongs in the contextual layer.
legacy_story: An island eaten for fertilizer. Britain annexed Banaba in 1900, the year phosphate was found, and the British Phosphate Commissioners, owned by Britain, Australia and New Zealand, strip-mined about 90% of its surface, shipping more than 20 million tonnes to Antipodean farms. In December 1945 the surviving Banabans were moved 2,000 km to Rabi Island in Fiji, bought with money from their own phosphate trust. Katerina Teaiwa calls it the literal consumption of a homeland, and the deposits ran out in 1979, as Kiribati became independent.

name: Posen & West Prussia
agents: German peasant colonist families recruited by the Settlement Commission
victims: Poles (Polacy)
summary: Posen & West Prussia, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: Imperial Germany tried to colonize its own Polish provinces and mostly failed. Bismarck's 1886 law created a Royal Settlement Commission with 100 million marks to buy Polish land for German farmers, and funding eventually topped 950 million marks. But of 438,000 hectares it acquired, only a quarter came from Polish owners, most bought from Germans, and Polish land banks out-competed it. By 1918 it had settled about 22,000 German families, far short of its aim. Its most durable product was the 1908 law letting the state expropriate Polish estates outright.

sources.title: Blanke 1981, Prussian Poland in the German Empire

name: Generalplan Ost
agents: Reich Germans (planned)
ethnic-German Volksdeutsche resettlers (at Zamość)
victims: Poles
Ukrainians
Belarusians
Russians
Balts
Jews (murdered in the Holocaust the plan presupposed)
summary: A genocidal settler-colonial plan with partial implementation, not a completed settler society.
omission_or_category_error: The attempted plan must be separated from the actually implemented expulsions, deportations, Germanization, mass murder, and settlement experiments under Nazi occupation.
legacy_story: The most murderous settlement plan ever drafted, and only partly carried out. Under Himmler, the agronomist Konrad Meyer's office designed Generalplan Ost to expel some 31 million people, far more in later versions, beyond the Urals and settle Germans in their place across Poland, Ukraine, Belarus and the Baltics. Implementation reached the Zamość region, where from November 1942 about 100,000 Poles, including 30,000 children, were driven from 297 villages to make room for ethnic-German settlers before the war turned.

name: French Algeria
agents: European settlers (pieds-noirs) of French, Spanish, Italian and Maltese origin
victims: Muslim Algerians (Arab and Amazigh communities)
summary: French Algeria, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: France invaded in 1830 and stayed 132 years, seizing land and political power while remaining a tenth of the population. The conquest itself was catastrophic, and Algeria's Muslim population fell by perhaps a third between 1830 and the 1870s through war, dispossession and famine. Europeans, the pieds-noirs, numbered about 984,000 by 1954, holding some 2.7 million hectares of the best farmland. When independence came in 1962, nearly the whole settler community left, around 650,000 in that year alone.

name: Italian Libya
agents: Italian colonists (the 1938 “Ventimila” and after)
victims: Cyrenaican Arab-Bedouin communities
summary: A qualified case. The demographic colonization was large but brief, cut off by the 1943 Allied conquest before it settled into a permanent society.
omission_or_category_error: Initial conquest, Cyrenaican camp deportations and mass death, Fascist demographic colonization, and wartime collapse should not be collapsed into one settlement phase.
legacy_story: Italy's settlement of Libya came after an atrocity. To break Cyrenaican resistance from 1929 to 1934, Badoglio and Graziani deported the population to sixteen concentration camps. Ali Abdullatif Ahmida documents more than 60,000 deaths, and Omar al-Mukhtar was hanged before a crowd in 1931. Only then did the Fascist “demographic colonization” begin, the Ventimila, 20,000 settlers shipped in one 1938 convoy into purpose-built villages, some 110,000 Italians by 1940. The Allied conquest of 1943 ended it.

name: Western Sahara
agents: Moroccan settlers
victims: Sahrawis
summary: The markers fall west of the berm, in the Moroccan-controlled zone.
omission_or_category_error: The 1975 invasion and refugee flight, wartime wall and mine displacement, subsidized Moroccan settlement, and continuing resource and housing policy require separate representation.
legacy_story: When Spain withdrew in 1975, Morocco moved in. King Hassan II's Green March sent some 350,000 civilians across the border, and the territory was partitioned. Within months tens of thousands of Sahrawis had fled to refugee camps near Tindouf in Algeria, whose population is disputed, with UNHCR planning figures near 90,000 and Polisario counts far higher. Morocco later presented the UN with lists of 120,000 settlers it had moved in since 1975. The UN still lists Western Sahara as a non-self-governing territory with no administering power, and M. Padrón Hernández argues it should be read as a settler colony.

name: Northern Cyprus
agents: Mainland Turkish settlers
victims: Greek Cypriots (displaced south)
Turkish Cypriots (moved north)
summary: Northern Cyprus, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: Turkey's 1974 invasion split the island and set two populations moving. About 160,000 to 180,000 Greek Cypriots fled south and 45,000 to 60,000 Turkish Cypriots north. Then came organized settlement. A 1975 labour protocol aimed to bring some 30,000 mainland Turks to farm the emptied north, and heavy settlement continued to 1977. The eventual settler total is fiercely disputed. The 2011 census counted 295,000 residents of every kind, Turkish Cypriots and the locally born children of settlers among them, and estimates of actual mainland settlers range widely, which is why the numbers, intent and the label all remain contested.

name: Iraqi Kurdistan & Kirkuk
agents: Arab families relocated from central and southern Iraq with state land and housing
victims: Kurds
Turkmen
Assyrians
summary: Iraqi Kurdistan & Kirkuk, as represented in the current atlas.
legacy_story: Baʼathist Iraq re-engineered its north by Arabization. From the mid-1970s some 250,000 Kurds and other non-Arabs were expelled from a wide belt of the north, their land and homes handed to Arab families moved up from the centre and south. The 1988 Anfal campaign under Ali Hassan al-Majid reached genocidal scale, and Human Rights Watch documents the disappearance of about 100,000 Kurds, with the chemical attack on Halabja killing roughly 5,000 in a day. The expulsions from Kirkuk continued until the regime fell in 2003.

name: Syrian Arab Belt
agents: ~4,000 Arab families displaced by the Tabqa Dam, settled 1975 in 41 model farms
victims: Kurds of al-Hasakah / Jazira
summary: Planning began in the 1960s. Implementation ran 1973–75 and was suspended in 1976, leaving the villages in place.
legacy_story: Syria planned an Arab cordon along its Kurdish north. In 1962 a special census had stripped some 120,000 Jazira Kurds of citizenship, and the 1965 “Arab Belt” scheme then envisaged an Arabized strip 15 km deep and 280 km long on the Turkish border. In 1975 the state settled about 4,000 Arab families, farmers displaced by the Tabqa Dam, in 41 model villages built on land taken from Kurds, many of them the very people denaturalized in 1962. Assad suspended the plan in 1976 but never dismantled the villages.

name: Israeli settlement of the occupied territories
agents: Israeli settlers (about 737,000 in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, about 29,000 on the Golan)
victims: Palestinians of the West Bank and East Jerusalem
Syrians of the Golan (the great majority expelled in 1967), including the remaining Druze
summary: This record covers the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan. It excludes the Gaza settlements removed in 2005.
legacy_story: In 1967 Israel occupied the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Syrian Golan, and built civilian settlements across all three under military rule and a separate legal geography. In the West Bank and East Jerusalem the UN's 2025 report counts 737,332 settlers and records 49 new outposts between November 2023 and October 2024, the most in any year on its record. On the Golan, where most of the Syrian population was driven out in 1967, about 29,000 settlers now live in 35 settlements alongside roughly 28,000 remaining Druze. In July 2024 the International Court of Justice, in an advisory opinion, held Israel's continued presence in the Palestinian territory unlawful, and the Golan annexation of 1981 had already been declared void by the UN Security Council. Israel disputes the framing.

name: Steppe migration into South Asia
agents: Steppe (Sintashta and Andronovo-related) pastoralists, ancestral Indo-Aryan speakers
victims: Indus Valley and Iranian-farmer-related populations of northwest South Asia
summary: An expansion case included as a language-and-elite turnover, a deliberate contrast to the demographic replacements of the same steppe world in Europe.
omission_or_category_error: Steppe ancestry and Indo-Aryan language spread are supported, but the atlas should not state a uniform subcontinental displacement event where regional mechanisms and demographic effects remain debated.
legacy_story: The same steppe world that transformed Europe sent a branch south. Around 2000 BCE, Sintashta-related pastoralists descended from the Central Asian steppe into the northwest of the subcontinent, layering onto the farming populations of the declining Indus civilization. Narasimhan and colleagues track the steppe ancestry arriving on that timeline and tie it to the spread of the Indo-Aryan languages and the Vedic world. Unlike in Europe, the newcomers stayed a minority everywhere, so this reshaped language and status more than the gene pool.

post_v5_retirement.reason: The broad migration row has no bounded land or resident-settlement outcome and fails the event-unit inclusion rule. Migration evidence is preserved; statistical inclusion is retired pending separately reviewed bounded successors.

name: Yayoi settlement of Japan
agents: Yayoi wet-rice farmers from the Korean peninsula
later Kofun-era continental migrants
victims: Jomon hunter-gatherers
summary: An expansion case read from ancient DNA, and a strong non-European case of farming-driven population turnover.
legacy_story: Japan's islands were held for millennia by the Jomon, hunter-gatherers with their own pottery and a deep genetic signature. From around 900 BCE, wet-rice farmers known as the Yayoi crossed from the southern Korean peninsula into Kyushu and spread northeast. Cooke and colleagues read the arrival as a massive influx that absorbed rather than erased the Jomon, followed by a further continental wave in the Kofun period. Jomon ancestry survives in modern Japanese at only about ten to fifteen percent, so the cumulative turnover was large even where each step was admixture.

name: Anglo-Saxon settlement of Britain
agents: Angles, Saxons, Jutes and Frisians from the North Sea coast
victims: Romano-British population of eastern and southern Britain
summary: A proto-historic case, the same migration-or-elite-transfer question the atlas raises for the Athabaskan case.
legacy_story: As Roman Britain fell apart, people from the North Sea coast, Jutland, Lower Saxony and Frisia, crossed into its eastern lowlands. The old question was whether a few warlords imposed a language on the Romano-British or whether whole communities moved in. Ancient DNA has tilted the answer toward migration. Gretzinger and colleagues find up to three quarters of the ancestry in eastern England came from the continental North Sea, though it varies sharply from place to place and mixes with the resident population. English begins here, in that settlement.

name: Magyar settlement of the Carpathian Basin
agents: Magyar (early Hungarian) conquerors
victims: Late Avar, Slavic and Romance-speaking inhabitants of the Carpathian Basin
summary: An expansion case. Language turnover by a demographic minority, a deliberate contrast to the replacement cases.
omission_or_category_error: The conquest and settlement are real, but evidence does not support depicting the basin as simply emptied or its diverse population uniformly displaced; elite incorporation, warfare, migration, and assimilation must be separated.
legacy_story: Around 895 CE a confederation of Uralic-speaking horsemen, the Magyars, rode into the Carpathian Basin and stayed. They came from the Ural region carrying Inner Asian ancestry, and they made the plain of the middle Danube Hungarian, a Uralic island in a Slavic and Romance sea. Maroti and colleagues find the conquering core did carry distinctive eastern ancestry, but they were few and were absorbed within generations. The language held even as the gene pool did not.

name: Numic spread across the Great Basin
agents: Numic (Uto-Aztecan) speakers, ancestral Shoshone, Paiute, Ute and Kawaiisu
victims: Fremont farmer-foragers and other pre-Numic Great Basin peoples
summary: An expansion case read from linguistics and archaeology, one Indigenous people spreading over another.
legacy_story: From a small homeland near the California-Nevada line, Numic-speaking people fanned out across the Great Basin over the last thousand years, the ancestors of the Shoshone, Paiute and Ute. As they spread they replaced the Fremont farmers and the other earlier peoples of the desert. It is the closest North American parallel to the Athabaskan migration, a documented ethnolinguistic turnover across a vast dry interior, ending only as horses and then settlers arrived from the east.

name: Kayenta migration into the southern deserts
agents: Kayenta migrants from the northern Southwest (ancestral Puebloan)
victims: Local Hohokam and San Pedro / Tonto Basin populations
summary: An expansion case, a rare instance where intrusive settlers left a clear material fingerprint among a host population.
legacy_story: When the northern Southwest emptied in the late 1200s, Kayenta people from north-eastern Arizona moved south and planted immigrant enclaves among the Hohokam and the peoples of the San Pedro and Tonto basins. At sites like Reeve Ruin and Davis Ranch they kept a distinct identity, their own perforated plates, entry-box kivas and technology, the cleanest archaeological signature of settlers who move in and hold themselves apart. The blended Salado world that followed grew out of that meeting.

name: Cahokian colonies on the northern frontier
agents: Cahokian / Middle Mississippian colonists
victims: Late Woodland peoples of the upper Mississippi (Wisconsin)
summary: An expansion case, a pre-Columbian colonial outpost planted and then abandoned.
legacy_story: Around 1050 CE, as the city of Cahokia rose on the Mississippi near modern St. Louis, its people planted colonies far to the north. At Trempealeau in western Wisconsin, seven hundred kilometres upriver, settlers transplanted Cahokia's mound-and-plaza town plan whole into Late Woodland country. The palisaded enclave at Aztalan followed. Pauketat and colleagues call Trempealeau a colony outright, intrusive people among locals, not just goods passed along a trade route.

name: Nahua (Pipil and Nicarao) migration into Central America
agents: Nahua-speaking migrants (Pipil and Nicarao) from central Mexico
victims: Maya, Lenca and Oto-Manguean (Chorotega) populations of Central America
summary: An expansion case, one of the most overlooked long-distance migrations in the Americas.
legacy_story: Long before the Spanish, Nahua-speaking people from central Mexico moved more than a thousand kilometres south into Central America. The Pipil settled western El Salvador and Guatemala, the Nicarao the Pacific shore of Nicaragua, founding lasting Nahua-speaking towns like Cuzcatlan among the resident Maya, Lenca and Chorotega. It was a folk migration that put down roots, not just a conquering dynasty.

name: Wari and Tiwanaku colonies in Moquegua
agents: Tiwanaku colonists from the Titicaca basin
Wari colonists from Ayacucho
victims: Resident Huaracane population of the middle Moquegua valley
summary: An expansion case, and the rare instance of two colonial powers settling one valley at once.
legacy_story: In the Moquegua valley of southern Peru, two Andean states planted colonies side by side. Tiwanaku, from the shores of Lake Titicaca, sent farmers six hundred kilometres downslope to build homeland temples and cemeteries at Omo and Chen Chen. Wari, from Ayacucho, seized the Cerro Baul mesa above them and cut a canal to green the desert, a rival enclave in sight of the first. Goldstein calls the Tiwanaku settlements a true diaspora, colonists who moved and stayed for centuries, not a garrison.

name: Saladoid settlement of the Caribbean
agents: Saladoid (Arawak-speaking) farmers from the lower Orinoco
victims: Archaic-age foragers of the Antilles (Ortoiroid and Casimiroid)
summary: An expansion case read from ancient DNA. It reframes the Caribbean's colonization as something that began millennia before 1492.
legacy_story: The Caribbean was colonized long before Columbus. From around 800 BCE, ceramic-making, cassava-farming people known as the Saladoid, Arawak speakers from the lower Orinoco, canoed up the island chain from Trinidad to Puerto Rico and Hispaniola. Ancient DNA now shows they did not blend with the archipelago's earlier foragers so much as replace them. Fernandes and colleagues find over ninety-eight percent of the ceramic-age ancestry was newcomer, with the older Archaic population surviving mainly in western Cuba.

sources.title: Keegan & Hofman 2017, The Caribbean before Columbus

name: Indonesian Transmigration
agents: State-sponsored Javanese, Madurese, Balinese and Sundanese settlers
victims: Dayak peoples of Kalimantan
Indigenous peoples of Sulawesi and Sumatra
summary: The clearest modern non-European settler program, run by an Asian state rather than an overseas empire. West Papua is treated as its own case.
omission_or_category_error: Dutch-era colonisatie, New Order mass transmigration, province-specific settlement frontiers, and later decentralized or spontaneous migration have different coercive and demographic effects.
legacy_story: For a century the state has moved poor farmers from crowded Java, Madura and Bali to Indonesia's outer islands and settled them on land that was already someone's. It began as Dutch kolonisatie in 1905 and became a vast program under Suharto, relocating millions onto forest and customary land in Sumatra, Kalimantan and Sulawesi. In Lampung the transmigrants became the majority. Dayak and other Indigenous peoples were pushed aside, and the resentment erupted in the Sampit killings of 2001.

name: Han colonization of the Yunnan frontier
agents: Han military colonists and civilian migrants
victims: Tai (Dai), Yi, Bai and Hani peoples of the south-west
summary: A frontier settler process distinct from the atlas's Inner Mongolia and Xinjiang cases, and thinner in the Tai-majority far south.
omission_or_category_error: Ming military colonies, Qing frontier administration and migration, mining booms, and suppression of local polities form multiple settlement waves over nearly five centuries.
legacy_story: Yunnan became part of China by settlement as much as by conquest. After the Ming took the south-west in 1382 they planted military-agricultural colonies, soldiers brought with their families, and civilian Han migrants followed for four centuries. The Tai, Yi, Bai and Hani were pushed into the uplands or absorbed as the basins around Kunming and Dali turned Han-majority. In the far south, among the Tai of Sipsong Panna, settlement stayed thin.

sources.title: Bin Yang 2009, Between Winds and Clouds

name: Tai-Ahom settlement of Assam
agents: Tai (Ahom) migrants from the upper Burma-Yunnan borderlands
victims: Bodo-Kachari, Chutiya, Moran and Borahi peoples of the Brahmaputra valley
summary: An eastern-India frontier case, a thin settler elite that endured and then assimilated.
legacy_story: In 1228 a Tai prince named Sukaphaa crossed the Patkai hills from the upper Burma borderlands into the Brahmaputra valley with a few thousand followers, and the order they built lasted six hundred years. The Ahom cleared wet-rice land, bound the local Bodo-Kachari, Chutiya and Moran into a corvee-settlement system, and slowly made Assam their own even as they themselves took on Hindu ways. A small warrior-migrant elite that reshaped a valley.

name: Burman settlement of the Irrawaddy
agents: Burman (Bamar) migrants from the northern uplands
victims: Pyu city-states and Mon of the lower Irrawaddy
summary: An expansion case whose founding narrative is itself contested scholarship.
omission_or_category_error: The case infers a long demographic settlement from language, archaeology, and state formation; it does not establish one bounded displacement event or clearly identify affected predecessor communities.
legacy_story: The Burmans entered the Irrawaddy from the northern hills in the ninth century and made its dry heartland their own. As they built Bagan and its thousands of temples, the old Pyu city-states faded and their people were absorbed, and the Mon of the south were subordinated. The valley that had been Pyu and Mon became Burman, the demographic core of Myanmar to this day.

name: Japanese Karafuto (southern Sakhalin)
agents: Japanese home-island settlers
state-assisted migrants for coal, timber and fisheries
victims: Ainu
Uilta (Orok)
Nivkh (Gilyak)
summary: Korean labourers, many brought under coercion, are counted apart from the settler population.
omission_or_category_error: Japanese settler colonization, Indigenous Ainu/Nivkh/Uilta dispossession, coerced Korean labor, and the 1945 Soviet takeover and population removals are distinct histories.
legacy_story: Japan took the southern half of Sakhalin from Russia in 1905 and made Karafuto a settler prefecture. Migrants poured in for the coal, timber and fisheries, and by the mid-1930s the population passed 300,000, overwhelmingly Japanese settlers, against roughly 2,000 Ainu, Uilta and Nivkh. Tessa Morris-Suzuki describes it as an overwhelmingly settler colony. The 1945 Soviet conquest ended it, and almost all the settlers were repatriated, the mirror image of the colony's rise.

name: Maasai expansion across the Rift Valley
agents: Maasai (Plains Nilotic pastoralists)
victims: Sirikwa and earlier highland peoples
Southern Cushitic pastoralists
Okiek (Dorobo) hunter-gatherers
Kwavi, Laikipiak and other defeated Maa sections
summary: An expansion case of the pastoralist age. The Nandi push into the Uasin Gishu is its tail end, and the British later took the same highlands as the Kenya Highlands.
legacy_story: The Maasai, Plains Nilotic pastoralists, spread south out of the Lake Turkana region across the Rift Valley from around the seventeenth century, taking the best grazing as they went. They moved into the stone-walled cattle country of the earlier Sirikwa, absorbed or drove off Southern Cushitic herders and Okiek hunter-gatherers, and in the nineteenth-century Iloikop wars the Maasai proper defeated and scattered rival Maa sections like the Kwavi and Laikipiak. Around 1850 they held a corridor from central Kenya to northern Tanzania, until the 1880s and 1890s brought rinderpest, smallpox and drought, the Mutai, and broke them.

sources.title: Waller 1985, Ecology, Migration and Expansion in East Africa (African Affairs)

name: Nandi expansion into the Uasin Gishu
agents: Nandi (Kalenjin, Southern Nilotic)
victims: Uasin Gishu Maasai (a defeated Maa section)
summary: The tail end of the Rift Valley pastoralist wars, on highlands the British soon took as the Kenya Highlands.
legacy_story: In the middle of the nineteenth century the Nandi, a Kalenjin people of the western highlands, took the Uasin Gishu plateau from the Uasin Gishu Maasai, one of the Maasai sections. That section had already been broken in the Maasai civil wars, and the survivors were finished by the rinderpest, smallpox and drought of the 1890s. The Nandi moved into the wreckage as much as they conquered it, and held the plateau until the British seized it for white settlers around 1906.

name: Ndebele conquest of the Shona plateau
agents: Ndebele (Khumalo Nguni) under Mzilikazi and Lobengula
victims: Shona and Kalanga chiefdoms of the plateau
the remnant Rozvi state
summary: A pre-colonial conquest the British settlement of Rhodesia then layered over. See the Southern Rhodesia case.
omission_or_category_error: The label reduces a sequence involving the Rozvi state, Kalanga communities, multiple Ndebele migrations, tribute relations, raids, and later colonial ethnic categories to a single Ndebele-versus-Shona event.
legacy_story: Fleeing Shaka's Zulu, Mzilikazi led his Ndebele across the Limpopo, and by 1840 had built a kingdom on the high country of what is now south-western Zimbabwe. The Ndebele settled Matabeleland, raided the Shona chiefdoms for cattle and captives, and ruled the plateau until a British column broke the kingdom in 1893 and took the land for the settlers of Rhodesia.

name: Oromo expansion into the Ethiopian highlands
agents: Oromo (Cushitic pastoralists of the gada system)
victims: Sidama and Damot peoples
frontier Amhara and Christian-kingdom populations
the southern reach of the sultanate of Adal
summary: An expansion case that reshaped the Ethiopian highlands before any European involvement.
omission_or_category_error: Two centuries of movement, alliance, adoption, conquest, assimilation, and state formation across a vast region cannot support a single displacement arrow or a single agent–victim story.
legacy_story: From about 1522 the Oromo, Cushitic pastoralists organized by the gada age-grade system, pushed north and west out of the southern lowlands into the heart of Ethiopia. Over two centuries they took much of the central highlands, settling on land emptied by the recent wars between the Christian kingdom and the sultanate of Adal, and displacing or absorbing Sidama, Damot and frontier Amhara. The sixteenth-century monk Bahrey wrote the first account of them, from the Christian side.

legacy_story: The Luo, River-Lake Nilotes, moved south out of the southern Sudan over several centuries and settled the eastern shore of Lake Victoria in what is now western Kenya. As they took the lakeshore and its fishing and grazing, they pushed the Bantu Gusii up into the highlands, absorbed other neighbours, and made Nyanza a Luo country.

name: Oorlam expansion into central Namibia

victims: Nama (Khoekhoe) chiefdoms

summary: A pre-colonial expansion German South West Africa then displaced. See the Namibia case.
legacy_story: Armed with guns, horses and ox-wagons from the Cape frontier, Afrikaans-speaking Oorlam commandos crossed the Orange River into central Namibia from the 1810s. Under Jonker Afrikaner they made Windhoek their base, subdued the Nama chiefdoms and fought the Herero for the central grazing lands through mid-century, running a raiding and cattle economy until German colonization overtook it after 1884.

sources.title: Lau 1987, Namibia in Jonker Afrikaner's Time

name: The Fulani jihad and the Sokoto Caliphate

legacy_story: In 1804 the Fulani scholar Usman dan Fodio launched a jihad against the Hausa kings, and within a decade his followers had overthrown the Hausa city-states and built the Sokoto Caliphate, the largest state in nineteenth-century Africa. Fulani emirs took the thrones, Fulani pastoralists pressed onto Hausa and Middle Belt land, and the caliphate raided the non-Muslim south for captives until the British conquered it in 1903.

legacy_story: Around 1050 the Fatimid rulers of Egypt loosed the Bedouin tribes of the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym westward into Ifriqiya as a punishment on a rebellious vassal. Tens of thousands of Arab nomads poured across North Africa over the following century, wrecking the Zirid towns, turning farmland to pasture, and spreading Arabic and Bedouin ways among the Amazigh. Ibn Khaldun, four centuries later, likened them to a swarm of locusts.

name: Spanish-ordered relocation of San Pedro Sobaipuri communities
mechanism: state-ordered partial relocation and mission concentration
agents: Governor José Tienda de Cuervo and Spanish frontier officers
Mission and presidio institutions seeking population, labor, and defense
Apache wartime pressure as the background security condition
victims: The documented subset of Sobaipuri-O'odham residents ordered from San Pedro Valley communities
summary: In early December 1761 Spanish officials decided to move Sobaipuri-O'odham residents from San Pedro communities to reinforce Soamca, Guevavi, and Bac, consolidate frontier defense, and bring more people under mission control. Captain Francisco Elías executed the order by March 1762 amid sustained Apache pressure. His report counted 250 people settled or enumerated at Tucson and said missionary and Indigenous officials had reported about 400; people not enumerated were described as moving among nearby towns. Thirty families are separately documented at Soamca, and activity is documented at Sonoita. These figures and places do not form one complete partition and are not combined. The order and substantial partial relocation are established; complete valley abandonment is not.
disputes: Sayre and Spicer describe an emptied lower San Pedro, while Seymour's archaeological interpretation reports O'odham occupations after 1762. The evidence supports substantial outward movement but leaves complete abandonment, durable exclusion, and Apache replacement unresolved. Soamca, Guevavi, and Bac were intended destinations; Tucson and Soamca are directly documented execution outcomes, while Sonoita and surrounding towns appear in the wider movement record. Spanish compulsion is the proximate mechanism; Apache pressure is an interacting condition.

name: Famine, raid, and abandonment of Las Humanas
agents: Drought, crop failure, famine, and disease
Spanish tribute, labor demands, mission institutions, and strategic consolidation

victims: Residents of Las Humanas / Gran Quivira
summary: Crop failure and food shortage struck Las Humanas from 1667. A contemporary Franciscan report attributed more than 450 deaths there to starvation in 1668, while the later NPS history describes the total more cautiously as perhaps 450. An Apache attack seriously damaged the mission in September 1670. The Franciscans probably closed it in 1671, and surviving residents moved through Abó toward Piro-speaking Rio Grande missions, probably Isleta, by 1672. Las Humanas was not durably replaced by an incoming community and remained abandoned until reoccupation of the area after 1800.
disputes: The death report, later population statements, and raid losses do not supply compatible denominators and cannot yield a mortality share or displacement total. Drought, famine, disease, Spanish extraction and consolidation, and Apache attack interacted. The evidence does not show a single-cause Apache conquest or replacement settlement.

victims: Residents of Quarai and Chililí
summary: Between late 1676 and early 1677 the Christian populations of Quarai and Chililí moved to Tajique amid famine, insecurity, and Spanish-Franciscan consolidation. Quarai residents carried a favored missionary's remains with them. Quarai and Chililí were not durably replaced by incoming communities. Tajique then failed as a destination, was abandoned shortly before the end of 1677, and was reoccupied in early 1678 by more than two hundred Indigenous families and a small garrison, remaining occupied at least through mid-1679. The Salinas district was therefore not continuously empty after 1678.

name: Danish-Norwegian mission-and-trade colonization of West Greenland
agents: The Danish-Norwegian Crown
Hans Egede and crown-backed mission institutions
Successive monopoly companies, merchants, and posted colonial personnel
victims: Kalaallit and other Inuit communities living near the West Greenland colony-town, mission, and trade network
summary: Beginning in 1721, Danish-Norwegian crown-backed missionaries and successive monopoly companies established a network of small colonial towns and mission-and-trade stations in West Greenland. These externally governed nodes exercised institutional control over land and organized trade and mission activity around nearby Kalaallit communities. European personnel remained few and were largely posted for fixed terms, while Greenlandic producers sustained the colonial trade. This was colonial incorporation, not mass European settler replacement.
disputes: The evidence does not establish coast-wide occupation, Indigenous tenure extinguishment, mass removal, or Indigenous cession. Danish-Norwegian elites justified the project partly through an asserted continuity with medieval Norwegian rule; that was a colonial rationale, not evidence of unbroken Scandinavian occupation or Kalaallit consent. A 1733 smallpox outbreak followed the return of a Greenlander from Denmark and caused severe local mortality around Godthåb, but the available account supplies no denominator for the affected network. The 1925 Ittoqqortoormiit movement, 1953–55 Inughuit removal, post-1782 separation and assimilation regimes, East Greenland's later incorporation, and later constitutional transitions occurred under later regimes and are not part of this 1721–1782 chronology.
omission_or_category_error: The retired medieval Norse settlement was not the eighteenth-century colonial project. The 1721 mission-and-trade network established externally governed territorial nodes among an existing Inuit population.
event_json_summary: Beginning in 1721, Danish-Norwegian crown-backed missionaries and successive monopoly companies established a network of small colonial towns and mission-and-trade stations in West Greenland. These externally governed nodes exercised institutional control over land and organized trade and mission activity around nearby Kalaallit communities. European personnel remained few and were largely posted for fixed terms, while Greenlandic producers sustained the colonial trade. This was colonial incorporation, not mass European settler replacement.

Landry’s introductory passage instead prints 1791, a disclosed conflict not used for the boundary. The French Archives nationales d’outre-mer independently identifies British domination beginning in 1793.
mechanism: British seizure and phased removal, followed by English fishing use; English abandonment when the French squadron appeared in 1796, French destruction of the town, and continued depopulation until French possession and resident settlement were re-established in 1816.
agents: Captain William Affleck and the British expedition and authorities; Rear-Admiral de Richery and the French squadron as the later 1796 destruction actor
victims: Seasonal fishermen and the French garrison removed immediately in 1793, followed by 950 resident inhabitants ordered evacuated in 1794; individual identities and complete destinations are not supplied.
summary: The sources support a distinct post-1783 population, phased 1793–1794 removal, later town destruction, and continued depopulation until re-established French settlement. Source conflict over the introductory date remains explicit rather than merging this sequence with 1778.
disputes: The sources do not provide a household roster, complete property-loss inventory, destination history for every deportee, compensation record, or measured livelihood effect.
event_json_summary: British seizure and phased resident evacuation followed by destruction and a durable wartime depopulated interval

mechanism: NKVD encirclement and roundup, truck movement to railheads, confinement in cattle cars, forced transport to special settlements, exile under special-settlement rules, later exemption from those rules, autonomy reorganization, and return.

victims: Pohl reports 37,713 Balkars exiled, while Helsinki Watch gives an estimated Balkar population of 42,666 at the time; the difference is preserved as a source-definition or denominator variance rather than reconciled.

disputes: The Pohl target does not establish the packet's 1957 return authorization, competing population denominator, detailed labor assignments, settlement list, household routes, return timing, or restitution; those remain unknown.

name: British-Indian (Hindostani) contract-worker migration to Suriname plantations, 1873–1916
date_resolution: The Nationaal Archief opening and index description directly define the British-Indian contract-worker migration window as 1873–1916. Hoefte's extract independently fixes the first Lalla Rookh arrival on 5 June 1873; the cited bodies do not give a more precise 1916 termination date.
mechanism: Transoceanic recruitment and migration under first contracts beginning on arrival, commonly five-year plantation labor obligations, possible re-contracting, and labor discipline backed by local ordinances and penal sanctions
agents: The Suriname colonial government as recruiting and contracting authority; plantation owners or managers as hirers and employers; British-Indian workers and the agents and officials administering their migration and contracts
victims: More than 34,000 Hindostani migrants from British India described by the archive as contract workers, including the first 399 indentured immigrants aboard the Lalla Rookh; the records also contain family and descendant information
summary: The sources independently identify the British-Indian cohort, recruitment channel, contracts, plantation destination, and coercive enforcement. Chinese and Javanese streams differ in origin, administration, and chronology, so the broad parent retires and the child receives a fresh profile.
disputes: The archive supports all domains while leaving the exact 1916 terminal act, individual contract and punishment outcomes, route variation, complete return pattern, and coercive effect across the full period unresolved.
